Hi everyone!

I'm relatively new here but have been working on an explicit continuous solution for the roots of the reduced Hilbert septic:

x⁷ + a x³ + b x² + c x + 1 = 0

The core idea is to express the roots as a chain of continuous one-variable functions (Kolmogorov–Arnold style) using polar decomposition and Re/Im separation.

Guiding Framework: Decoding Complex Objects

M = x + i y (or M = r e^{iθ}) naturally splits into two complementary domains:

Re — Local / Radial / Multiplicative Side

Aspect Keywords Mathematical Domain
Focus Local, Radii, Modulus Lorentz (c² - s² = 1)
Direction Contraction → -∞
Key Figure Hardy —
Operation Multiplicative Product
Goal Disassemble —

Im — Global / Phase / Additive Side

Aspect Keywords Mathematical Domain
Focus Global, Phase, Argument Euclid (c² + s² = 1)
Direction Expansion → +∞
Key Figure Euler —
Operation Additive Sum
Goal Construct —

The Great Purifier:
log = type purifier
log(M) = log r + i θ
→ Perfectly separates modulus (Re) from argument (Im) and turns products into sums.

Bridge: PDE ↔ ODE via the imaginary unit.

Application to Hilbert13

  • Polar substitution x = r e^{iθ}
  • Im(F) = 0 factors via Chebyshev: sin θ · Q(r, cos θ) = 0 → quartic in cos θ
  • Re(F) = -b gives modulus closure
  • Results in an explicit chain: (a,b,c) → r → C → θ → x

Repo: https://github.com/beanapologist/Hilbert13
(The full Mermaid diagram and cheatsheet are in the README.)

I’d love any feedback on the Lean formalization, the approach, or possible ways to push this further! I hope the explicit construction and Re/Im framework might offer useful intuition or a stepping stone toward the algebraic case.

Thanks!
Sarah
My feedback is "that code looks like it was written by AI and posting slop is against the terms and conditions of this site"
Thank you for your honesty. I'm still learning.

It's difficult if you are someone who is genuinely interested in learning. AI is such an appealing tool and it can usually get something compiling but sometimes the code quality is terrible. Learning lean is quite a steep curve and right now it's not clear to the community whether the fact that AI can just blast through stuff is an advantage or a disadvantage when it comes to learning. There's a theory which says that all the blood sweat and tears which everyone had to go through to get things working if they tried learning lean last year or before was actually the way people learnt.

My experience with LLMs is that by far the most fruitful interactions I've had with them is on topics in which I'm already an expert.

Understood. For me, Hilbert septic was less about the problem and more about analyzing complex objects by examining the real vs. imaginary dualities. Lean + AI offered a vehicle to check whether I was on the right track.
